blocks.text: Leviticus 8 records Moses carrying out the LORD's commands for the consecration of Aaron and his sons. The congregation witnesses their washing, clothing, anointing, sacrifices, and the application of blood to Aaron's ear, hand, and foot. They then eat at the tent of meeting and remain there for seven days, keeping the LORD's charge until their consecration is complete.

sections.title: The consecration of Aaron and his sons

blocks.text: The chapter locates priestly service in the wilderness tabernacle setting. The repeated movement between the congregation, the altar, and the tent of meeting shows that the inauguration concerns the people’s worship as well as Aaron and his sons personally.

The supplied context describes Israel's priesthood in terms of covenant holiness, sacrificial service, instruction, and guarding sacred space. Those functions help explain why this chapter includes both the priests' ritual preparation and their strict seven-day restriction at the tent of meeting: the office is being set apart for service in a holy setting.

The consecration matters because priesthood is presented as service on behalf of the worshiping community: priests mediate access, bless the people, teach holiness, and guard sacred space. Leviticus 8 therefore gives ritual form to the responsibilities that will govern Aaron's and his sons' ministry.

Leviticus moves from sacrifice and priestly inauguration into instructions about purity, the Day of Atonement, holy communal life, sacred time, land, covenant consequences, and vows. Leviticus 8 is thus the beginning of a broader movement from establishing worship to ordering the life of the community around holiness.

sections.title: From priestly inauguration to holy communal life
